newsitem.title: USA: Fed's Phillips urges broad US financial regulation.
newsitem.headline: Fed's Phillips urges broad US financial regulation.

text.p: If Congress decides to tear down the legal barriers separating banking from other financial service industries, a comprehensive regulator like the Federal Reserve would still be required, Fed Governor Susan Phillips said on Monday.

In the ongoing legislative debate over financial reform, some proposals suggest that no comprehensive regulator is necessary. A bank regulator would oversee a company's bank activities, for example, while a securities regulator would monitor the company's securities activites.

But Phillips, in a speech to the Institute of International Bankers, backed a regulatory scheme included in other proposals that would create an overall or "umbrella" financial regulator to monitor diversified companies from the top down.
Such a regulator's role would be similiar to the role of the Fed in monitoring bank holding companies under the present system, she said in a prepared speech.
"There are those who argue that umbrella supervision of a diverse financial services holding company would either be an impossible task or an intolerable burden," Phillips said.

"But the risk-analysis and surveillance techniques that we have decided are the most effective for bank holding companies should also be adaptable to more diverse financial organizations that include banking operations," she said.
Companies that intend to offer various financial services with only token banking activity have complained that bank-like umbrella supervision would be excessive.
Phillips said such companies might be granted an exemption or "carve-out" from umbrella supervision.
But she suggested such companies might also benefit from comprehensive regulation.

"To be successful, a financial services company should reap synergy gains not only by marketing a variety of products to customers but also by pooling and jointly managing diverse financial risks," Phillips said. "It is those policies and risks that an umbrella supervisor must understand in order to gauge the risks to the insured institution."

Under some legislative proposals, banks would be allowed to have direct subsidiaries engaging in non-bank activities. Under other proposals, banks would have to segregate non-bank activities by creating affiliates under a holding company structure.
Phillips said a holding company structure was needed to prevent banks from gaining an unfair competitive advantage as a result of federal deposit insurance and other factors.
"I think it difficult to deny that banks and their subsidiaries benefit from a federal subsidy, and benefit in ways that an affiliate of the bank does not," she said.
Rules have been proposed to prevent a subsidiary from gaining such benefits, but "that subsidy transfer cannot be eliminated," Phillips said.
